```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c

import funs
from funs import DSText

import spacy

ub = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/"
```

```{python}
#| tags: [remove]
#| include: false
ub = ""
```

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
docs = (
    pl.read_parquet(ub + "data/imdb5k_pca.parquet")
    .select(c.id, c.label, c.text)
    .rename({"id": "doc_id"})
    .sort(c.doc_id)
    .group_by(c.label, maintain_order=True)
    .head(100)
    .with_columns(
        text = c.text.str.replace_all("<br />", " ")
    )
)
```

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
```

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
anno = DSText.process(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.text), nlp)
```

### Questions

`docs` and `anno` hold the same 200 IMDb movie reviews as the last notebook, 100
labeled `"positive"` and 100 labeled `"negative"`, with the `<br />` already
replaced by a space.

Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save
it to a variable.

1. Filter `anno` to the first sentence of the first review (`doc_id` equal to
`"doc0001"` and `sid` equal to 1) and select the columns `tid`, `token`, `lemma`,
and `is_alpha`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.doc_id == "doc0001", c.sid == 1)
    .select(c.tid, c.token, c.lemma, c.is_alpha)
)
```

The comma and the period are the only tokens with `is_alpha` equal to `false`.

2. Filter `anno` to the alphabetic tokens with `.filter(c.is_alpha)`, count the
number of times each `lemma` appears, sort from most to least common, and keep the
first 10 rows.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
    .head(10)
)
```

All ten are short, common words such as "the", "be", and "and".

3. Take the code from the previous question and draw it as a bar plot with
`geom_col`, with `lemma` on the x-axis and the count on the y-axis. Add
`coord_flip()` so the labels are readable.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
    .head(10)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lemma, c.n))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
)
```

4. Filter `anno` to the alphabetic tokens with `.filter(c.is_alpha)`. Then add a
column `next_token` equal to `c.lemma.shift(-1).over([c.doc_id, c.sid])`. Select
the columns `doc_id`, `sid`, `lemma`, and `next_token`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .with_columns(
        next_token = c.lemma.shift(-1).over([c.doc_id, c.sid])
    )
    .select(c.doc_id, c.sid, c.lemma, c.next_token)
)
```

The last word of each sentence has a missing `next_token`, because `.over()`
stops the shift at the end of each sentence. In the first sentence, that word is
"good".

5. Take the code from the previous question (without the `.select`). Remove the rows
where `next_token` is missing with `.filter(c.next_token.is_not_null())`, and then
add a column `bigram` equal to `c.lemma + " " + c.next_token`. Select `doc_id`,
`sid`, and `bigram`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .with_columns(
        next_token = c.lemma.shift(-1).over([c.doc_id, c.sid])
    )
    .filter(c.next_token.is_not_null())
    .with_columns(
        bigram = c.lemma + " " + c.next_token
    )
    .select(c.doc_id, c.sid, c.bigram)
)
```

6. Take the code from the previous question and count the number of times each
`bigram` appears. Sort from most to least common and keep the first 15 rows.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .with_columns(
        next_token = c.lemma.shift(-1).over([c.doc_id, c.sid])
    )
    .filter(c.next_token.is_not_null())
    .with_columns(
        bigram = c.lemma + " " + c.next_token
    )
    .group_by(c.bigram)
    .agg(count = pl.len())
    .sort(c.count, descending=True)
    .head(15)
)
```

The most common bigrams are pairs of very common words, such as "of the" and
"be a". Only "this movie" and "the film" tell us that these are movie reviews.

7. The block below is given. It follows the chapter's steps to compute the PMI of
every bigram and saves the result as `pmi`, with one row per bigram. Run it and look
at the table.

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
bigrams = (
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .with_columns(
        next_token = c.lemma.shift(-1).over([c.doc_id, c.sid])
    )
    .filter(c.next_token.is_not_null())
    .with_columns(
        bigram = c.lemma + " " + c.next_token
    )
)

word_counts = (
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(word_count = pl.len())
)

total_words = word_counts.select(c.word_count.sum()).item()
total_bigrams = bigrams.height

pmi = (
    bigrams
    .group_by(c.bigram, c.lemma, c.next_token)
    .agg(bigram_count = pl.len())
    .join(
        word_counts.rename({"lemma": "w1", "word_count": "w1_count"}),
        left_on=c.lemma,
        right_on=c.w1
    )
    .join(
        word_counts.rename({"lemma": "w2", "word_count": "w2_count"}),
        left_on=c.next_token,
        right_on=c.w2
    )
    .with_columns(
        p_bigram = c.bigram_count / total_bigrams,
        p_w1 = c.w1_count / total_words,
        p_w2 = c.w2_count / total_words
    )
    .with_columns(
        pmi = (c.p_bigram / (c.p_w1 * c.p_w2)).log()
    )
    .select(c.bigram, c.bigram_count, c.pmi)
)
pmi
```

8. Sort `pmi` from the largest to the smallest value of `pmi` and keep the first 15
rows.

```{python}
(
    pmi
    .sort(c.pmi, descending=True)
    .head(15)
)
```

Every one of these bigrams appears only once. When two rare words show up next to
each other a single time, the PMI is as large as it can be.

9. Do the same as the previous question, but first keep only the bigrams with
`bigram_count` of at least 5.

```{python}
(
    pmi
    .filter(c.bigram_count >= 5)
    .sort(c.pmi, descending=True)
    .head(15)
)
```

With at least 5 uses, the list makes more sense: names ("New York", "Cathy Lee"),
movie vocabulary ("sci fi", "low budget", "special effect"), and phrases from the
reviewer's voice ("my opinion", "my favorite").

10. Filter `anno` to the tokens that are part of a named entity
(`c.ent_type != ""`) and select the columns `doc_id`, `token`, `ent_type`, and
`ent_iob`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.ent_type != "")
    .select(c.doc_id, c.token, c.ent_type, c.ent_iob)
)
```

Every token of a multi-word entity gets the same `ent_type`. The first token has
`ent_iob` equal to `"B"` and the others have `"I"`, as with "Costas Mandylor" in
the first review.

11. Take the code from the previous question (without the `.select`). Add a column
`entity_id` equal to `(c.ent_iob == "B").cum_sum().over(c.doc_id)`. Then group by
`doc_id`, `entity_id`, and `ent_type`, and join the tokens back together with
`entity_text = c.token.str.join(" ")`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.ent_type != "")
    .with_columns(
        entity_id = (c.ent_iob == "B").cum_sum().over(c.doc_id)
    )
    .group_by(c.doc_id, c.entity_id, c.ent_type)
    .agg(entity_text = c.token.str.join(" "))
)
```

12. Take the code from the previous question, keep only the `PERSON` entities, and
count the number of times each `entity_text` appears. Sort from most to least common
and keep the first 15 rows.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.ent_type != "")
    .with_columns(
        entity_id = (c.ent_iob == "B").cum_sum().over(c.doc_id)
    )
    .group_by(c.doc_id, c.entity_id, c.ent_type)
    .agg(entity_text = c.token.str.join(" "))
    .filter(c.ent_type == "PERSON")
    .group_by(c.entity_text)
    .agg(count = pl.len())
    .sort(c.count, descending=True)
    .head(15)
)
```

The top two names each come from a single review. Kornbluth is the director of
the movie in one review, and Baird is a character in another. A name that one
review repeats many times can top the list.

13. Take the code from question 11 and count the number of entities of each
`ent_type`. Draw the result as a bar plot with `geom_col` and `coord_flip()`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.ent_type != "")
    .with_columns(
        entity_id = (c.ent_iob == "B").cum_sum().over(c.doc_id)
    )
    .group_by(c.doc_id, c.entity_id, c.ent_type)
    .agg(entity_text = c.token.str.join(" "))
    .group_by(c.ent_type)
    .agg(count = pl.len())
    .ggplot(aes(c.ent_type, c.count))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
)
```

`PERSON` is by far the most common type, followed by `ORG`, `CARDINAL`, and `GPE`.
Reviews use a lot of numbers, such as a rating out of ten.

14. Filter `anno` to the first sentence of the first review (`doc_id` equal to
`"doc0001"` and `sid` equal to 1) and select the columns `tid`, `token`, `dep`, and
`head_idx`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.doc_id == "doc0001", c.sid == 1)
    .select(c.tid, c.token, c.dep, c.head_idx)
)
```

The subject "movie", the word "not", and the adjective "good" all have
`head_idx` equal to 7, which points to the verb "is".

15. Find the most common subject-verb pairs. Filter `anno` to the subjects
(`dep` equal to `"nsubj"`) and select `doc_id`, `sid`, `subject = c.lemma`, and
`verb_idx = c.head_idx`. Join this to the verbs on `doc_id`, `sid`, and `verb_idx`,
where the verbs are
`anno.filter(c.upos == "VERB").select(c.doc_id, c.sid, verb_idx = c.tid, verb = c.lemma)`.
Count the pairs of `subject` and `verb`, sort, and keep the first 10 rows.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.dep == "nsubj")
    .select(
        c.doc_id, c.sid,
        subject = c.lemma,
        verb_idx = c.head_idx
    )
    .join(
        anno.filter(c.upos == "VERB").select(
            c.doc_id, c.sid, verb_idx = c.tid, verb = c.lemma
        ),
        on=[c.doc_id, c.sid, c.verb_idx]
    )
    .group_by(c.subject, c.verb)
    .agg(count = pl.len())
    .sort(c.count, descending=True)
    .head(10)
)
```

Almost every pair has `I` or `you` as the subject. Reviews are written in the
first person, so the reviewer is the most common subject.

16. Find the most common adjective-noun pairs in the same way. Filter `anno` to
`dep` equal to `"amod"` and select `doc_id`, `sid`, `adjective = c.lemma`, and
`noun_idx = c.head_idx`. Join this to the nouns (`upos` equal to `"NOUN"`), using
`noun_idx = c.tid` and `noun = c.lemma`. Count the pairs, sort, and keep the first 10
rows.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.dep == "amod")
    .select(
        c.doc_id, c.sid,
        adjective = c.lemma,
        noun_idx = c.head_idx
    )
    .join(
        anno.filter(c.upos == "NOUN").select(
            c.doc_id, c.sid, noun_idx = c.tid, noun = c.lemma
        ),
        on=[c.doc_id, c.sid, c.noun_idx]
    )
    .group_by(c.adjective, c.noun)
    .agg(count = pl.len())
    .sort(c.count, descending=True)
    .head(10)
)
```

"good movie" and "bad movie" are the two most common pairs.

17. Run `DSText.kwic()` on the lemma `"acting"` with `window=5` and `max_num=10`.

```{python}
DSText.kwic(anno, "acting", max_num=10, window=5)
```

"acting" appears next to "terrible" and "decidedly bad", but also next to
"good acting" and "above average". Reading the context shows how each reviewer
judged the acting.

18. Count the number of `"!"` tokens in each review, using
`n_excl = (c.token == "!").sum()` inside of `.agg`. Join to the labels and find the
average of `n_excl` for each `label`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .agg(n_excl = (c.token == "!").sum())
    .join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on=c.doc_id)
    .group_by(c.label)
    .agg(n_excl = c.n_excl.mean())
)
```

Negative reviews have more than twice as many
exclamation points on average (1.21) as positive ones (0.52).
